Signs of Termite Infestation — What to Look For

By Shaw's Pest Control  ·  Wichita, KS

What Are the Signs of Termite Infestation in Your Home?

If you're noticing strange damage to your woodwork or seeing small winged insects near your windows, you're right to be concerned. The signs of termite infestation are often subtle until significant damage has already occurred — especially in Kansas, where subterranean termites are the primary culprits. These pests work quietly behind walls and beneath floors, often going undetected for years. At Shaw's Pest Control, we've been identifying and eliminating termite problems across Wichita and surrounding communities since 1987, and our Master Tech-certified team knows exactly what to look for. In this guide, we'll walk you through the telltale signs that termites have moved into your home, what each warning signal means, and when it's time to call for a professional inspection.

Why Termite Damage Often Goes Unnoticed Until It's Serious

Subterranean termites — the species most common in Kansas — build their colonies underground and travel through mud tubes to reach wood sources in your home. Unlike drywood termites that live inside the wood they consume, subterranean termites maintain contact with soil for moisture, making them harder to detect from the surface.

The real problem is their feeding pattern. Termites eat wood from the inside out, leaving a thin veneer of timber or paint on the surface while hollowing out the structural support behind it. By the time visible damage appears, they may have been feeding for months or even years. A single colony can contain hundreds of thousands of termites, and they work 24 hours a day without stopping.

This is why regular inspections are critical, especially in older homes or properties with crawl spaces. Many homeowners discover termite damage only during renovations or when a piece of trim literally crumbles in their hands. At that point, the cost of repairs often far exceeds what prevention or early treatment would have required.

The Five Primary Signs of Termite Infestation

Understanding what to look for can help you catch an infestation before structural damage becomes severe. Here are the most reliable indicators that termites are active in your home:

Mud tubes on foundation walls or joists. These pencil-width tunnels are made of soil, wood particles, and termite saliva. They run along concrete foundations, floor joists, or walls, providing protected highways for termites to travel between their colony and food sources. If you break open a tube and find small, creamy-white insects inside, you have an active infestation.

Hollow-sounding wood. Tap on door frames, baseboards, or exposed beams with the handle of a screwdriver. If it sounds hollow or papery, termites may have eaten away the interior. You might also notice wood that sounds different from adjacent areas or feels unusually light.

Discarded wings near windows or doors. Reproductive termites (swarmers) emerge in spring to start new colonies. After landing, they shed their wings in small piles. Finding these wings indoors is a clear sign that a colony has matured nearby and is producing new reproductives — a sign the infestation has been established for at least three to five years.

Termite frass (droppings). While subterranean termites don't typically leave visible droppings, if you do encounter small piles of wood-colored pellets near wood or small holes, you may be dealing with drywood termites. However, in Kansas, this is less common than subterranean activity.

Visible swarmers. Seeing winged termites indoors, especially in spring, is one of the most definitive signs of an infestation. Swarmers are often mistaken for flying ants, but termites have straight antennae, equal-length wings, and a thick waist, while ants have elbowed antennae and pinched waists.

If you notice any of these signs, it's time to schedule a professional inspection. Our team provides thorough termite control in Wichita and can determine the extent of activity in your home.

What to Do When You Spot These Warning Signs

The moment you identify potential signs of termite infestation, don't wait to take action. Termites cause billions of dollars in damage across the United States every year, and most homeowners insurance policies don't cover termite damage because it's considered preventable.

Start by documenting what you've found — take photos of mud tubes, damaged wood, or discarded wings. Avoid disturbing the area too much, as this can help a pest control professional assess the severity and location of the colony. Don't attempt DIY treatments with hardware store sprays; these may kill visible termites but won't address the colony, and can actually cause termites to relocate to other areas of your home, making professional treatment more difficult.

Contact a licensed pest control company with termite expertise. At Shaw's Pest Control, our technicians hold three state certifications and use proven treatment methods tailored to Kansas termite species. A proper inspection includes checking crawl spaces, basements, attics, and exterior perimeters for activity and conducive conditions like moisture problems or wood-to-soil contact.

Treatment options vary based on the severity of the infestation. Liquid termiticides create a barrier in the soil around your home, while baiting systems target the colony directly. For active infestations, we often recommend a combination approach. You can learn more about treatment methods on our termites page.

Timing matters. Termites don't take vacations, and delaying treatment only gives them more time to damage your home's structure. Spring and early summer are peak swarming seasons, making them ideal times for inspections even if you haven't seen obvious signs yet.

Termite Risks in Wichita and South-Central Kansas

Wichita's climate — with hot summers, moderate winters, and periodic moisture from thunderstorms — creates favorable conditions for subterranean termites. The soil composition in south-central Kansas also supports termite colonies, particularly in areas with clay-heavy soil that retains moisture.

Homes built on slab foundations or with crawl spaces are particularly vulnerable. Older neighborhoods in Wichita, where homes may have settled or developed small foundation cracks over decades, provide easy entry points for termite mud tubes. Even newer construction isn't immune; termites can exploit gaps around plumbing penetrations or where concrete hasn't fully sealed.

If you're buying or selling a home in the Wichita area, a termite inspection should be non-negotiable. Many real estate transactions in Kansas include a termite inspection clause, and for good reason — an undetected infestation can derail a sale or leave a new homeowner with unexpected repair costs.

Regular monitoring is your best defense. Annual inspections catch problems early, and preventive treatments can protect your home before termites ever arrive.

Frequently Asked Questions

What do termite mud tubes look like?

Termite mud tubes are narrow tunnels, typically about the width of a pencil or slightly wider, made from soil, wood particles, and termite saliva. They're usually tan or brown and run along foundation walls, in crawl spaces, or across concrete surfaces. These tubes protect termites from predators and dry air as they travel between their underground colony and wood sources in your home.

How can you tell the difference between termite damage and water damage?

Termite damage leaves wood hollow with a honeycomb pattern inside, and you may find mud-like material or termite droppings nearby. Water damage typically causes wood to darken, warp, or feel spongy, often with visible mold or mildew. If you tap termite-damaged wood, it sounds hollow and may collapse easily, while water-damaged wood usually remains structurally intact longer but feels soft.

What time of year do termites swarm in Kansas?

Subterranean termites in Kansas typically swarm in spring, most commonly from March through May when temperatures warm and humidity rises. Swarms often occur on warm days following rain. Seeing winged termites indoors during this period indicates an established colony nearby. However, different termite species may swarm at other times, so any swarming activity warrants immediate inspection.

Can you have termites without seeing signs?

Yes, termites can cause significant damage without visible signs, especially subterranean termites that work inside walls and beneath floors. A colony may feed for years before homeowners notice mud tubes, hollow wood, or swarmers. This is why professional inspections are essential, particularly for homes with crawl spaces or older construction where termites have more hidden access points.

Are termites more active at certain times of day?

Termites work continuously, 24 hours a day, year-round. They don't sleep or take breaks, which is why a single colony can cause substantial damage relatively quickly. However, you're most likely to see termite swarmers during daylight hours in spring, as they're attracted to light and emerge during warmer parts of the day to establish new colonies.

What's the difference between termites and flying ants?

Termites have straight, bead-like antennae, four wings of equal length, and a broad, thick waist connecting their thorax and abdomen. Flying ants have elbowed antennae, two sets of wings with the front pair longer than the back, and a distinctly pinched waist. If you see swarming insects indoors and aren't sure which you're dealing with, save a few specimens for professional identification.
